Consistency.justification: The proposal closely follows the stated idea: it uses change-in-quantile features from three-phase currents, recurrence plots and RQA descriptors, an InceptionTime-based model, ReliefF, and the requested semi-supervised methods for fault detection, location, and phase identification on PV-connected transmission lines. It also includes PSCAD/EMT-style studies, WSCC 9-bus and IEEE 39-bus systems, converter operating modes, and relevant abnormal conditions. The hypothesis, abstract, experiments, and risks are internally coherent. Minor gaps include inconsistent emphasis on a 100 MW PV plant located at the line midpoint versus protection of the segment between a grid and a PV plant, and a hypothesis focused on faults with resistance up to 25 ohms while the experiment matrix extends to 50 ohms without specifying whether this is an out-of-scope stress test.

Clarity.justification: The research objective, pipeline, baselines, variants, metrics, and principal risks are presented clearly and in a logical sequence. The proposal gives unusually concrete scenario variables, hardware metrics, ablations, and reproducibility targets. However, important operational details remain ambiguous: the exact definition and aggregation of the mean change in quantiles, the quantile levels and window lengths, recurrence-plot embedding parameters and thresholding, the architecture used to fuse RQA and waveform features, the outputs used for localization and phase identification, and the decision logic connecting the quantile-CUSUM trigger to the learned classifier. It is also unclear whether InceptionTime receives raw recurrence matrices, RQA descriptors, temporal feature sequences, or some combination. These omissions prevent the method from being immediately reproducible.

Novelty.justification: The proposal offers a notably original integration of adaptive quantile change detection, recurrence-based representations, InceptionTime, feature selection, semi-supervised learning, and relay-hardware evaluation. Targeting relay-grade latency and very low false-trip rates while supplying fixed-point implementations is a valuable systems-oriented contribution. Nevertheless, most individual components are established methods, so the novelty is primarily in their combination and application rather than in a fundamentally new learning or protection principle. The claim that no current approach combines all components is plausible but is not supported by a systematic literature comparison or citations. The proposal should explain why this particular combination creates more than an additive engineering improvement and distinguish itself from recent hybrid signal-processing and deep-learning protection schemes.

Soundness.justification: The proposal has several sound elements: diverse EMT scenarios, conventional and learned baselines, component ablations, deterministic seeds, hardware measurements, fixed-point comparisons, and reporting of both median and tail latency. However, substantial methodological details are missing. A single-ended current-only method may face identifiability limitations for accurate fault localization, especially across fault resistance, source impedance, and inverter controls, yet this is not analyzed. Data splitting by random waveform could cause severe leakage among simulations generated from the same topology or parameter setting; topology-, controller-, event-, and seed-disjoint evaluation is needed. Semi-supervised label propagation can also leak test-distribution information unless the transductive protocol is carefully isolated. The rare-event validation is particularly under-justified: replaying 10 million seconds represents only about 0.32 years and cannot directly validate a target of 0.0001 false trips per year. An effective sample size of 100000 under importance sampling does not by itself establish unbiased tail estimates; proposal distributions, likelihood ratios, dependence assumptions, diagnostics, and confidence-interval coverage must be specified. The selected block-bootstrap length is asserted rather than justified, and the quantile estimator, CUSUM update, recurrence construction, calibration procedure, and statistical comparison tests are not mathematically defined. Thus, the plan is promising but not yet rigorous enough to substantiate its strongest safety-critical claims.

Feasibility.justification: The EMT simulations, HIL replay, classical baselines, ablations, and supervised learning experiments are implementable with current tools. Measuring latency, memory, and fixed-point error on embedded targets is also practical. The main difficulty is simultaneously computing streaming quantiles, recurrence representations, RQA features, and an InceptionTime model within a one-cycle decision budget on Cortex-M-class hardware. Recurrence matrices have quadratic cost in the window length, while a standard InceptionTime network may exceed embedded memory and computation budgets unless aggressively compressed. No model size, window length, operation count, memory budget, pruning strategy, or early-exit design is provided. The breadth of the scenario matrix and the long-background rare-event study will also require substantial simulation and verification resources. Feasibility would improve with explicit resource budgets, a staged hardware target, complexity analysis, and a fallback lightweight classifier.

Significance.justification: Reliable protection around converter-interfaced generation is an important and growing power-system problem because inverter controls alter fault-current magnitude and dynamics and can undermine conventional relay assumptions. A validated single-ended method that reduces misoperations while retaining cycle-level speed could have meaningful operational and safety benefits. The proposed reproducible EMT/HIL benchmark, calibration workflow, and embedded implementation could also be useful contributions independent of whether the full model wins. The impact is moderated by the current dependence on simulated and replayed data, uncertain transfer to unseen inverter firmware and network topologies, the limited treatment of high-impedance faults, and the absence of a concrete field-pilot or certification pathway. Therefore, the work has strong potential but is not yet demonstrably transformative.

strengths: Strong alignment with the proposed research idea and a coherent hybrid pipeline combining complementary transient representations and supervised or semi-supervised learning.

Comprehensive experimental ambition, including multiple networks, inverter modes, instrument-transformer nonidealities, conventional and learned baselines, ablations, HIL replay, fixed-point analysis, and embedded latency measurements.
Addresses an important safety-critical problem created by increasing penetration of converter-interfaced photovoltaic generation.
Explicitly recognizes generalization, rare-event estimation, hardware, security, and certification risks rather than ignoring them.
weaknesses: Core algorithmic details, including quantile definitions, recurrence parameters, feature fusion, model outputs, trigger-confirmation logic, and training protocols, are insufficiently specified for reproduction.

The proposed rare-event experiment cannot directly validate a false-trip target of 0.0001 per year, and the importance-sampling design lacks the assumptions and diagnostics required for credible extrapolation.
Single-ended current-only fault localization may be poorly identifiable across changing system and inverter conditions, but no observability analysis or voltage-assisted comparison is proposed.
Meeting a one-cycle deadline on Cortex-M hardware with recurrence processing and InceptionTime is uncertain without explicit complexity, memory, compression, and worst-case latency budgets.
Evaluation protocols do not yet guarantee topology-, controller-, scenario-, and seed-disjoint testing or prevent leakage through semi-supervised learning.
